blogs.title: The Pivoting Expert: When Contradictory Testimony Fails the Substantial Evidence Test
blogs.description: An analysis of the Federal Circuit's decision regarding the ’134 patent, focusing on the dangers of relying on expert testimony that contradicts itself during trial. This post will discuss the 'substantial evidence' standard and how an expert's failure to consistently map a claim limitation—particularly when attempting to 'pivot' in response to cross-examination—can render a jury's infringement verdict unsustainable at the JMOL stage.

blogs.title: Identifiable vs. Unique: The Nuances of Counting Signals in Patent Claims
blogs.description: This post explores the court's interpretation of the ’775 patent's requirement for 'three signals S1, S2, and S3.' It will analyze the critical legal distinction the court drew between signals being 'separately identifiable' versus 'unique,' and discuss why the court found that amending a claim from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' did not necessarily constitute a clear and unambiguous disavowal of scope regarding products with only two unique inputs.

blogs.title: The Mapping Gap: Why Technical Documentation is Not a Substitute for Expert Proof
blogs.description: A deep dive into the court's reversal of the ’775 patent verdict based on the failure to precisely map accused functionality to claimed limitations. The post will discuss the necessity of a rigorous one-to-one mapping of technical operations (in this case, the number of multiplications) and the court's refusal to allow a patentee to 'fill the gaps' of an expert's testimony through appellate briefing.
